blocks.text: NAFDAC, NEPA, okada, smog, brunch, flu. Every one of those words was manufactured — from initials, from two words fused together, or from a longer word cut short. English grows by assembling parts, and once you know the parts you can work out the meaning of a word you have never seen.

blocks.markdown:
### Affixation: prefixes and suffixes

A **prefix** goes in front of a root and changes its **meaning**:
> *happy* → **un**happy, *interpret* → **mis**interpret, *social* → **anti**social

A **suffix** goes after a root and usually changes its **word class**:
> *science* → scient**ific** (adjective), *strength* → strength**en** (verb), *advertise* → advertise**ment** (noun)

That difference is the key to most exam questions: decide first what word class the blank needs, then choose the suffix that produces it.

blocks.caption: Prefixes and the meanings they add

blocks.title: The negative prefix changes shape
blocks.text: *In-* becomes *im-* before m and p (*impossible*), *ir-* before r (*irregular*, *irrefutable*) and *il-* before l (*illegal*). Choosing the wrong shape — *inregular*, *inlegal* — is a frequent error, so let the first letter of the root guide you.

blocks.caption: Suffixes and the word classes they create

blocks.title: Filling a derivation blank
blocks.prompt: Complete the sentence with the correct form of *science*: "The committee demanded ______ evidence before reaching a conclusion."

steps.text: Look at what follows the blank. The next word is the noun *evidence*.
Ask what kind of word can stand in front of a noun and describe it. Only an adjective can.
List the forms available from the root: *science* (noun), *scientist* (noun for a person), *scientific* (adjective), *scientifically* (adverb).
Read the sentence back to confirm: 'The committee demanded scientific evidence before reaching a conclusion.'
Check the spelling of the derived form, since the root often changes: *science* loses its final e and gains -ific.

blocks.answer: scientific — an adjective is required because the blank modifies the noun *evidence*

blocks.markdown:
### Five other ways English makes words

**Compounding** — joining two whole words: *blackboard*, *bus stop*, *mother-in-law*.

**Blending** — fusing parts of two words: *smoke + fog = smog*, *breakfast + lunch = brunch*, *motor + hotel = motel*.

**Clipping** — shortening one word: *influenza → flu*, *laboratory → lab*, *examination → exam*.

**Acronyms and initialisms** — building from initial letters: *NAFDAC* and *NEPA* are pronounced as words, while *BBC* and *ATM* are spelled out letter by letter.

**Conversion** — moving a word to a new class with no change of form: *water* the noun becomes *water* the verb; *text* the noun becomes *text* the verb.

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: When a question gives you a root word and a blank, do not guess the suffix. Identify the word class the blank needs by looking at the words on either side of it, and only then choose the form. Half the wrong answers in this question type are the right root in the wrong class.

points: Prefixes change meaning; suffixes usually change word class.
The negative prefix *in-* changes shape to im-, ir- or il- depending on the root's first letter.
Decide which word class the blank requires before choosing a suffix.
Compounding joins whole words, while blending fuses parts of two words.
Clipping shortens one word; acronyms are built from initial letters.
Conversion moves a word into a new class without changing its form.
Some derivations are irregular, such as *wise* to *wisdom* and *free* to *freedom*.
